summary.title: Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy
summary.authors: P. Nemes – Incze, Z. Kónya, I. Kiricsi, Á. Pekker, Z.E. Horváth, K. Kamarás, L.P. Biró
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the critical challenge of sample instability in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) when characterizing functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Functional groups weaken the van der Waals forces anchoring tubes to substrates, causing them to be swept away by the STM tip during scanning. The authors propose a novel immobilization strategy by embedding functionalized multiwalled CNTs into a few-layer graphene (FLG) composite, effectively clamping the tubes to prevent movement. Using Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS), the researchers successfully mapped energy-resolved tunneling conductance on these stable samples. The results reveal that acid-based functionalization preferentially occurs along the zigzag crystallographic direction of large-diameter CNTs. Furthermore, the study distinguishes between globally p-doped regions (due to acid adsorption) and locally modified regions where functionalization destroys the sp2 lattice, leading to low conductance and loss of atomic resolution. The work demonstrates that CITS provides unique insights into local doping levels, charge transfer, and defect creation that are invisible to standard topographic imaging.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the critical challenge of sample instability in Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) when characterizing functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Functional groups weaken the van der Waals forces anchoring tubes to substrates, causing them to be swept away by the STM tip during scanning. The authors propose a novel immobilization strategy by embedding functionalized multiwalled CNTs into a few-layer graphene (FLG) composite, effectively clamping the tubes to prevent movement. Using Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS), the researchers successfully mapped energy-resolved tunneling conductance on these stable samples. The results reveal that acid-based functionalization preferentially occurs along the zigzag crystallographic direction of large-diameter CNTs. Furthermore, the study distinguishes between globally p-doped regions (due to acid adsorption) and locally modified regions where functionalization destroys the sp2 lattice, leading to low conductance and loss of atomic resolution. The work demonstrates that CITS provides unique insights into local doping levels, charge transfer, and defect creation that are invisible to standard topographic imaging.

Research Context
Sidewall functionalization alters CNT electronic properties. Global spectroscopic methods lack spatial resolution. STM offers atomic-scale spatial resolution. Sample instability prevents reliable STM measurements. Functional groups weaken tube-substrate adhesion. STM tips can physically displace unstable nanotubes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a FLG composite stabilize functionalized CNTs for STM? Does functionalization prefer specific crystallographic directions? Can CITS map local doping and charge transfer? Will immobilization allow reproducible energy-resolved maps? Do functional groups destroy the sp2 lattice locally?

Methodological Details
CNTs were prepared via chemical vapor deposition. Catalysts used were Co/Fe supported on alumina. Functionalization involved three chemical steps. Acid treatment used H2SO4/HNO3 mixture. Treatment duration was 24 hours at room temperature. Groups were transformed to COCl using SOCl2. Diaminopropane was used for final cross-linking. Defects were confirmed by increased D/G ratio. Immobilization used a CNT – FLG composite. Composite was made into a buckypaper. Suspension was filtered through a polycarbonate membrane. Filter pore size was 200 nm. Electrical contact was made with carbon colloid paste. STM used a Multimode III SPM (Veeco). Mode of operation was CITS. Data processing was done using Scilab. Probes were mechanically cut Pt/Ir wire. Atomic resolution used 500 pA current and 100 mV bias. Topography/CITS used 300 pA current and 300 mV bias. TEM used a Philips CM20 microscope. TEM operated at 200 keV.

Procedures And Architectures
CNTs were embedded between FLG flakes. FLG layer clamps the nanotube to prevent movement. Graphite and MWCNTs have similar work functions. No significant substrate doping is expected. CITS acquires STS curves at each pixel. Conductance maps plot dI/dV vs bias voltage. Maps were displayed at -160 mV bias voltage. LDOS maps correlate with conductance maps. Atomic resolution images show superstructure patterns. Superstructures indicate electron scattering from defects. Functionalized regions appear as surface protrusions. Low conductance regions lack atomic resolution. LDOS minimum maps show Fermi level shifts. Global p-doping shifts Fermi level by ~0.25 eV.

Key Results
STM tip movement displaces functionalized CNTs. FLG composite successfully immobilizes CNTs. Functionalization increases surface defect concentration. Acid treatment causes p-doping of CNTs. Global p-doping shifts chemical potential positively. Functionalized regions show lower tunneling conductance. Low conductance correlates with sp2 lattice destruction. Functionalization follows the zigzag crystallographic direction. Oxidation prefers specific crystallographic directions. High conductance regions are free of defects. Atomic resolution is lost in functionalized bands. LDOS minimum maps reveal local doping variations. Asymmetric dI/dV curves indicate impurity states. Charge transfer shifts dI/dV minimum negatively. Functional groups do not perturb but alter the lattice.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CITS reveals features invisible to topography. Local functionalization state is energy-dependent. In situ studies of gas sensing are now possible. Adsorption processes can be better understood. Zigzag direction preference confirms theoretical models. Charge transfer creates local Coulomb potentials. sp3 conversion reduces delocalized π electrons. Global doping arises from acid adsorption. Local doping variations indicate charge transfer.

Contradictions And Limitations
Impurity states near Fermi level were not found. Theory predicts impurity states for monovalent groups. Interpretation is difficult in low conductance regions. Electronic structure of damaged surface is unknown. Superstructure patterns extend from defect sites. Conversion of COCl to amide was not complete. IR spectra show residual carboxyl groups.

Claims
Functionalized CNTs can be stabilized for STM using a FLG composite. Movement is restricted by the clamping FLG layer. Composite provides a stable sample.  Reliable CITS measurements become possible.
Acid functionalization preferentially occurs along the zigzag direction. Functionalized regions follow the zigzag direction. Measurements provide evidence for direction preference.  Oxidation mechanisms are direction-dependent.
Functionalization destroys the sp2 lattice, causing low conductance. Low conductance arises from lattice destruction. Atomic resolution is lost in these regions.  Electronic structure is fundamentally altered.

Data And Code Availability
STM images and STS curves are presented. Data was processed using Scilab.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Reproducible STS spectra were required for tips. Atomic resolution on graphite was a selection criterion.

Key Figures Tables
Fig 1 shows CNT movement during STM scanning. Fig 2 shows Raman and IR spectra of samples. Fig 3 illustrates the CNT – FLG composite. Fig 4 shows STM images and conductance maps. Fig 5 shows atomic resolution and functionalized bands. Fig 6 details dI/dV maps and LDOS minimum.

Three Takeaways
FLG composite enables stable STM of functionalized CNTs. Functionalization follows the zigzag crystallographic direction. CITS reveals local doping and lattice destruction.
